query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Elevated temperatures can promote the rapid formation of a dense, adherent Fe3O4-rich passive oxide layer on the surface of pre‐exposure Q235 steel that suppresses further corrosion degradation in harsh, chloride‐containing environments, compared to the less uniform oxide scale (rich in Fe2O3) that forms at room temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state with its inherent microstructural and surface properties.
generation.intervention: Expose identically prepared Q235 steel samples to a corrosive medium (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) at room temperature versus elevated temperature (e.g., 80–100 °C) without any additional coatings or surface treatments.
generation.conditions: Laboratory immersion tests under controlled environmental conditions at a fixed exposure time, with one group kept at room temperature (∼25 °C) and another at a moderate elevated temperature (80–100 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: The composition, thickness, and uniformity of the surface oxide layer (specifically the formation of Fe3O4 versus Fe2O3 phases).
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, enhanced diffusion and oxidation kinetics favor the rapid development of a continuous Fe3O4 passive layer. This layer is denser and more adherent, thereby limiting the penetration of aggressive chloride ions into the underlying metal. In contrast, at room temperature a less uniform, potentially porous oxide mixture (with more Fe2O3) forms, which is less protective and allows higher corrosion rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to room temperature samples, those exposed at elevated temperatures will exhibit a thicker, predominantly Fe3O4 oxide layer, along with lower corrosion current densities and higher electrochemical impedance values, indicating improved corrosion resistance.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel samples exposed at room temperature in the same corrosive medium.
generation.boundary: This protective mechanism is expected to hold within a moderate elevated temperature range; temperatures that are too high or thermal cycling conditions may disrupt the continuity or adhesion of the protective oxide layer, negating its beneficial effect.
generation.uncertainty: While the general effect of temperature on oxidation kinetics is well established, the exact phase balance between Fe3O4 and Fe2O3, the precise protective quality of the resulting oxide layers, and the long‐term stability of the passive film in actual service conditions require further in-depth electrochemical and microstructural investigations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple identical Q235 steel specimens that are pre-cleaned to remove any initial surface oxides. Immerse them in a standardized 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under two temperature conditions (room temperature at ∼25 °C and elevated temperature at 80–100 °C) for a fixed time period. Conduct electrochemical measurements (potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) at regular intervals. After exposure, analyze the surface oxide compositions and morphologies using X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy with energy dispersive spectroscopy (SEM-EDS).
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and phase composition via XRD
Surface morphology and continuity via SEM-EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the elevated temperature samples do not form a significantly thicker, more uniform Fe3O4-rich oxide layer than the room temperature samples, or if the elevated temperature samples show equal or higher corrosion current densities and lower impedance (i.e. higher corrosion rates) relative to the room temperature controls, then the hypothesis that elevated temperature induces a protective passive layer would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, CrMnFeCoNi HEA coatings with different ZrC contents were prepared on Q235 steel by a PTA process, and the effects of ZrC on the morphology, composition, hardness, friction, and corrosion properties of the coatings were investigated.

In this paper, the CoCrFeNiTix HEA coatings are prepared on Q235 steel substrate by laser cladding. The effect of Ti content on the microstructure and corrosion resistance in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution was studied. Furthermore, the corrosion resistance mechanism was analyzed experimentally and by first-principles calculations.
